title: Psalms Chapter 90 Quiz - Multi-Level
description: An enhanced quiz on Psalms chapter 90 with Easy, Medium, Hard, and Theological levels. Each level has 15 carefully crafted questions. Choose your difficulty and dive in!

easy.title: Psalms Chapter 90 Quiz - Easy Level
easy.description: Perfect for beginners! Test your basic knowledge of Psalms Chapter 90.

questions.question: In Psalms 90, which of the following appears FIRST in the chapter?
options: Lord, thou hast been our dwelling place in all generations
Thou carriest them away as with a flood
For a thousand years in thy sight are but as yesterday
questions.correctAnswer: Lord, thou hast been our dwelling place in all generations
questions.explanation: This phrase appears first in Psalms 90:1, which is the opening verse of the chapter.

questions.question: Who is described as the man of God in Psalms 90?
questions.explanation: Psalms 90:1 identifies the author as Moses the man of God.

questions.question: According to Psalms 90, what has been our dwelling place in all generations?
questions.explanation: Psalms 90:1 states, 'Lord, thou hast been our dwelling place in all generations.'

questions.question: Before what were the mountains brought forth, according to Psalms 90?
options: Before the earth and the world were formed
questions.correctAnswer: Before the earth and the world were formed
questions.explanation: Psalms 90:2 says, 'Before the mountains were brought forth, or ever thou hadst formed the earth and the world.'

questions.question: How long is God described as existing in Psalms 90?
options: Since the creation of the earth
questions.explanation: Psalms 90:2 states God exists 'even from everlasting to everlasting.'

questions.question: What does God do to man, according to Psalms 90?
options: Givest man dominion over the earth
questions.explanation: Psalms 90:3 says, 'Thou turnest man to destruction.'

questions.question: What command does God give to the children of men in Psalms 90?
questions.explanation: Psalms 90:3 includes God saying, 'Return, ye children of men.'

questions.question: How does God view a thousand years, according to Psalms 90?
options: As yesterday when it is past
questions.correctAnswer: As yesterday when it is past
questions.explanation: Psalms 90:4 says, 'For a thousand years in thy sight are but as yesterday when it is past.'

questions.question: What is a thousand years compared to, besides yesterday, in Psalms 90?
options: As a watch in the night
questions.correctAnswer: As a watch in the night
questions.explanation: Psalms 90:4 states, 'and as a watch in the night.'

questions.question: How does Psalms 90 describe the carrying away of people?
options: As on the wings of an eagle
questions.explanation: Psalms 90:5 says, 'Thou carriest them away as with a flood.'

questions.question: In Psalms 90, people are compared to what in the morning?
questions.explanation: Psalms 90:5 states, 'in the morning they are like grass which groweth up.'

questions.question: True or False: Psalms 90 says that in the evening, the grass is cut down and withereth.
questions.explanation: Psalms 90:6 states, 'In the morning it flourisheth, and groweth up; in the evening it is cut down, and withereth.'

questions.question: True or False: Psalms 90 calls Moses a man of God.
questions.explanation: Psalms 90:1 refers to Moses as 'the man of God.'

questions.question: True or False: Psalms 90 says that God formed the earth and the world before the mountains were brought forth.
questions.explanation: Psalms 90:2 says, 'Before the mountains were brought forth, or ever thou hadst formed the earth and the world,' indicating the mountains were before the earth and world formed is not stated.

questions.question: True or False: Psalms 90 says that a thousand years in God's sight are like a mountain that never changes.
questions.explanation: Psalms 90:4 compares a thousand years to 'yesterday when it is past' and 'a watch in the night,' not to a mountain.

medium.title: Psalms Chapter 90 Quiz - Medium Level
medium.description: Ready for more? Apply biblical truths from Psalms Chapter 90 to real-life situations.

questions.question: According to Psalms 90:7, what causes us to be consumed and troubled?
questions.explanation: Psalms 90:7 states, 'For we are consumed by thine anger, and by thy wrath are we troubled,' showing that God's anger and wrath are the cause.

questions.question: What does Psalms 90:12 promise will happen if someone learns to number their days as commanded in Psalms 90:11?
options: They may apply their hearts unto wisdom
They will be consumed by wrath
They will not fear the Lord
questions.correctAnswer: They may apply their hearts unto wisdom
questions.explanation: Psalms 90:11 speaks of the fear of the Lord and his wrath, and Psalms 90:12 follows by promising that if we learn to number our days, we may apply our hearts to wisdom.

questions.question: What does Psalms 90:10 say about the typical length of human life?
options: The days of our years are threescore years and ten
All our days are as a tale that is told
We are consumed by thine anger
Our secret sins are before thee
questions.correctAnswer: The days of our years are threescore years and ten
questions.explanation: Psalms 90:10 clearly states, 'The days of our years are threescore years and ten,' indicating the typical lifespan.

questions.question: How does Psalms 90:8 explain the visibility of our sins in relation to God's presence, connecting to Psalms 90:7?
options: Our secret sins are in the light of thy countenance
Our sins are hidden from God
Our sins are unknown to God
questions.correctAnswer: Our secret sins are in the light of thy countenance
questions.explanation: Psalms 90:8 explains that God has set our iniquities before Him and our secret sins are in the light of His countenance, connecting to the reason in Psalms 90:7 why we are consumed by His anger and wrath.

questions.question: What practical lesson can believers take from the fact that 'all our days are passed away in thy wrath' (Psalms 90:9)?
options: To seek God's mercy and live wisely
To ignore the passing of time
To rely on human strength alone
questions.correctAnswer: To seek God's mercy and live wisely
questions.explanation: Psalms 90:9 highlights the brevity and difficulty of life under God's wrath, prompting believers to seek mercy and live wisely.

questions.question: According to Psalms 90:12, why is it important to number our days?
options: So that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom
So that we may increase in strength
So that we may avoid sorrow
So that we may extend our years
questions.correctAnswer: So that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom
questions.explanation: Psalms 90:12 directly states the purpose of numbering our days is to apply our hearts to wisdom.

questions.question: What does Psalms 90:11 reveal about the relationship between the fear of God and His wrath?
options: According to the fear of God, so is his wrath
God’s wrath is unrelated to fear
God’s wrath is less than human fear
questions.correctAnswer: According to the fear of God, so is his wrath
questions.explanation: Psalms 90:11 says, 'even according to thy fear, so is thy wrath,' indicating a direct link between the reverence or fear of God and the measure of His wrath.

questions.question: How does Psalms 90:10 describe the experience of the strength during the longest days of life?
options: Their strength is labour and sorrow
Their strength is joy and peace
questions.correctAnswer: Their strength is labour and sorrow
questions.explanation: Psalms 90:10 explains that even if life extends to fourscore years, their strength is labour and sorrow.

questions.question: What does it mean practically to be 'consumed by thine anger' as in Psalms 90:7?
options: To suffer the consequences of sin and God's displeasure
To be physically consumed by fire
To be indifferent to God's wrath
questions.correctAnswer: To suffer the consequences of sin and God's displeasure
questions.explanation: Being 'consumed by thine anger' (Psalms 90:7) means experiencing the effects of God's displeasure due to sinfulness.

questions.question: Why does Psalms 90:9 compare our years to a tale that is told?
options: Because our lives are brief and pass quickly
Because our lives are long and detailed
Because our years are full of joy
questions.correctAnswer: Because our lives are brief and pass quickly
questions.explanation: Psalms 90:9 uses the metaphor of a tale that is told to illustrate the brevity and fleeting nature of human life.

questions.question: How should understanding the brevity of life in Psalms 90:10 influence a believer's daily living?
options: Encourage living wisely and valuing each day
Encourage relying only on physical strength
questions.correctAnswer: Encourage living wisely and valuing each day
questions.explanation: The recognition that life is 'soon cut off' (Psalms 90:10) should motivate believers to live wisely and cherish each day.

questions.question: What role does awareness of God's anger and wrath play in spiritual growth according to Psalms 90:7-8?
options: It prompts repentance and seeking God's mercy
It encourages hiding sins from God
It leads to ignoring God's commands
questions.correctAnswer: It prompts repentance and seeking God's mercy
questions.explanation: Psalms 90:7-8 shows that God's anger is directed at sin, which should lead believers to repent and seek mercy rather than despair or concealment.

questions.question: How does the knowledge that 'a thousand years are but as yesterday' in God's sight (Psalms 90:4) shape our understanding of human life in Psalms 90:9-10?
options: It highlights the fleeting nature of human life compared to God’s eternity
It means human life is eternal
It implies God ages like humans
questions.correctAnswer: It highlights the fleeting nature of human life compared to God’s eternity
questions.explanation: Psalms 90:4 contrasts God's eternal nature with the brevity of human life described in Psalms 90:9-10, emphasizing how short human life is.

questions.question: True or False: Psalms 90:12 teaches that numbering our days leads to applying our hearts to wisdom.
questions.explanation: Psalms 90:12 explicitly states that teaching us to number our days results in applying our hearts unto wisdom.

questions.question: True or False: Psalms 90:7 says that we are comforted by God's anger and wrath.
questions.explanation: Psalms 90:7 states we are consumed and troubled by God's anger and wrath, not comforted.

hard.title: Psalms Chapter 90 Quiz - Hard Level
hard.description: Challenge yourself with deep analysis and cross-biblical connections from Psalms Chapter 90.

questions.question: What does the psalmist ask the Lord to do in Psalms 90:13?
options: Teach us to number our days
questions.explanation: In Psalms 90:13, the psalmist implores the Lord to return, indicating a desire for divine intervention and mercy.

questions.question: According to Psalms 90:14, what does the psalmist desire early in the day?
questions.explanation: Psalms 90:14 expresses a longing for the Lord's mercy to be granted early so that the people may rejoice throughout their days.

questions.question: In Psalms 90:15, what does the psalmist request in relation to their afflictions?
questions.explanation: Psalms 90:15 asks for gladness in proportion to the days of affliction they have endured, indicating a desire for restoration.

questions.question: What does Psalms 90:16 ask the Lord to let appear to His servants?
questions.explanation: In Psalms 90:16, the psalmist petitions for the Lord's work and glory to be revealed to His servants and their children.

questions.question: What does the psalmist ask God to establish in Psalms 90:17?
questions.explanation: Psalms 90:17 requests that God establish the work of the hands of His people, emphasizing the importance of fruitful labor.

questions.question: In which verse does the psalmist ask the Lord to return?
questions.explanation: The request for the Lord to return is clearly stated in Psalms 90:13, reflecting a yearning for divine presence.

questions.question: What does the Hebrew word 'hesed' in Psalms 90:14 mean?
questions.explanation: 'Hesed' refers to God's loving-kindness or mercy, which the psalmist seeks early in the day in Psalms 90:14.

questions.question: Which literary device is prominent in Psalms 90:14, where the psalmist expresses a desire for mercy?
questions.explanation: The structure of Psalms 90:14 employs parallelism, emphasizing the connection between mercy and rejoicing.

questions.question: Which other Bible passage connects to the theme of God's mercy as seen in Psalms 90:14?
questions.explanation: Ephesians 2:4 speaks of God's great mercy, resonating with the psalmist's plea for early mercy in Psalms 90:14.

questions.question: Which other Bible passage connects to the theme of human affliction as expressed in Psalms 90:15?
questions.explanation: Romans 5:3-4 discusses glory arising from tribulations, which parallels the request for gladness amidst affliction in Psalms 90:15.

questions.question: What verse precedes Psalms 90:13?
questions.explanation: Psalms 90:12, which speaks of numbering our days, directly precedes the request for the Lord to return in Psalms 90:13.

questions.question: What comes after Psalms 90:15?
questions.explanation: Psalms 90:16 follows directly after Psalms 90:15, continuing the theme of God’s glory and work.

questions.question: The plea for God's beauty in Psalms 90:17 reflects a desire for what?
questions.explanation: The beauty of the Lord signifies His presence among His people, as requested in Psalms 90:17.

questions.question: True or False: Psalms 90 emphasizes the brevity of human life.
questions.explanation: Psalms 90 discusses the fleeting nature of life, especially in verses 10 and 12, highlighting the importance of numbering our days.

questions.question: True or False: The entire chapter of Psalms 90 is attributed to David.
questions.explanation: Psalms 90 is specifically noted as a prayer of Moses, not David, as stated in the first verse.

theological.title: Psalms Chapter 90 Quiz - Theological Level
theological.description: Deep biblical theology from Psalms Chapter 90 that unites all believers. Explore foundational truths about God, creation, and humanity.

questions.question: What doctrine does Psalms 90:2 teach about God's nature?
options: God is eternal, existing from everlasting to everlasting
God is limited by creation and time
God is dependent on the world for existence
God is mutable and changes over time
questions.correctAnswer: God is eternal, existing from everlasting to everlasting
questions.explanation: Psalms 90:2 states, 'even from everlasting to everlasting, thou art God,' affirming God's eternal, unchanging nature.

questions.question: What doctrine does Psalms 90:3 teach about human sin and mortality?
options: Humanity is subject to destruction and called to repentance
Humanity is inherently immortal and unchanging
Sin has no effect on human mortality
Humans are independent of divine judgment
questions.correctAnswer: Humanity is subject to destruction and called to repentance
questions.explanation: Psalms 90:3 says, 'Thou turnest man to destruction; and sayest, Return, ye children of men,' showing human mortality linked to sin and the call to repent.

questions.question: What doctrine about human life span and divine judgment is taught in Psalms 90:10?
options: Human life is limited with toil and sorrow under divine judgment
Human life span is unlimited and free from suffering
God rewards humans with eternal life regardless of sin
Human strength guarantees a long and joyful life
questions.correctAnswer: Human life is limited with toil and sorrow under divine judgment
questions.explanation: Psalms 90:10 explains that human days are limited and marked by labor and sorrow, reflecting the consequences of divine judgment.

questions.question: Which divine attribute does Psalms 90:4 specifically demonstrate?
questions.explanation: Psalms 90:4 states, 'For a thousand years in thy sight are but as yesterday when it is past,' highlighting God's eternal nature transcending time.

questions.question: Which divine attribute does Psalms 90:7 specifically demonstrate?
questions.explanation: Psalms 90:7 says, 'For we are consumed by thine anger, and by thy wrath are we troubled,' emphasizing God's attribute of just wrath against sin.

questions.question: How does Psalms 90 prepare for New Testament teachings on human frailty and divine eternity?
options: By contrasting transient human life with God’s eternal nature
By denying human mortality in favor of spiritual immortality
By emphasizing human independence from God
By teaching universal salvation without repentance
questions.correctAnswer: By contrasting transient human life with God’s eternal nature
questions.explanation: The Psalm contrasts human mortality with God's eternal existence (Psalms 90:2,4), a theme echoed in New Testament teachings on human frailty and divine eternity.

questions.question: What redemptive-historical connection does Psalms 90:12 establish with wisdom literature?
options: The call to number our days to gain wisdom aligns with Proverbs’ emphasis on fearing the Lord
It rejects wisdom as irrelevant for salvation
It emphasizes human wisdom over divine revelation
It teaches that wisdom is unnecessary because of predestination
questions.correctAnswer: The call to number our days to gain wisdom aligns with Proverbs’ emphasis on fearing the Lord
questions.explanation: Psalms 90:12 urges 'teach us to number our days...that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom,' echoing Proverbs’ doctrine that wisdom begins with the fear of the Lord.

questions.question: What combined doctrine do verses Psalms 90:8 and Psalms 90:9 teach about sin and divine judgment?
options: God’s omniscience exposes all sins, resulting in a life spent under His wrath
Sin is hidden from God and has no consequences
God ignores secret sins but judges public ones
Human sinfulness is unrelated to divine wrath
questions.correctAnswer: God’s omniscience exposes all sins, resulting in a life spent under His wrath
questions.explanation: Verse 8 states God sets our secret sins before Him, while verse 9 shows our days pass in God’s wrath, together teaching God’s all-knowing judgment on sin.

questions.question: What combined doctrine do Psalms 90:14 and Psalms 90:15 teach about God's mercy and human suffering?
options: God’s mercy satisfies and brings gladness even amidst affliction
God’s mercy removes all human suffering permanently
Human suffering is a sign of God’s rejection without hope
Mercy and suffering are unrelated in God’s dealings
questions.correctAnswer: God’s mercy satisfies and brings gladness even amidst affliction
questions.explanation: Verses 14 and 15 request satisfaction with mercy so that gladness may arise despite affliction and evil seen, underscoring God’s merciful presence in suffering.

questions.question: What combined doctrine do Psalms 90:16 and Psalms 90:17 teach about God’s work and human response?
options: God’s work and glory should be evident in His people, and He establishes their efforts
Human works are independent of God’s influence
God’s glory is hidden from His servants and their children
God rejects human labor and does not bless it
questions.correctAnswer: God’s work and glory should be evident in His people, and He establishes their efforts
questions.explanation: Verses 16 and 17 ask that God’s work and glory appear to servants and their children and that He establish their work, showing divine blessing on human labor.

questions.question: Sceptics claim that Psalms 90:7-10 presents a harsh, unforgiving God who condemns all humanity without hope. What does the passage actually teach?
options: That while God’s wrath is real and humanity is mortal, the Psalm calls for repentance and mercy
That God is indifferent and uninvolved in human affairs
That all humans are predestined to wrath without any call for repentance
That God’s wrath is a myth and does not affect human life
questions.correctAnswer: That while God’s wrath is real and humanity is mortal, the Psalm calls for repentance and mercy
questions.explanation: Verses 7-10 acknowledge God’s wrath and human mortality but the Psalm also calls for repentance (v.3,13) and mercy (v.14), showing a compassionate God.

questions.question: What doctrine does Psalms 90:1 teach about God’s providence and covenant faithfulness?
options: God is the eternal dwelling place and refuge for all generations
God abandons His people across generations
God’s presence is temporary and unreliable
God only cares for the current generation
questions.correctAnswer: God is the eternal dwelling place and refuge for all generations
questions.explanation: Verse 1 calls God 'our dwelling place in all generations,' affirming His providential care and covenant faithfulness across time.

questions.question: Which divine attribute does Psalms 90:11 specifically demonstrate?
questions.explanation: Verse 11 asks, 'Who knoweth the power of thine anger?' highlighting God’s attribute of wrath and its fearful power.

questions.question: What combined doctrine do Psalms 90:5 and Psalms 90:6 teach about human life and divine judgment?
options: Human life is transient and fragile, like grass cut down by divine judgment
Human life is eternal and unaffected by God
God’s judgment only affects the wicked, sparing the righteous
Human life grows stronger with each day regardless of God’s will
questions.correctAnswer: Human life is transient and fragile, like grass cut down by divine judgment
questions.explanation: Verses 5 and 6 compare human life to grass that flourishes in the morning and withers by evening, underlining transience and divine sovereignty.

questions.question: How does Psalms 90:13-14 reflect the biblical theme of prayer for divine mercy amid suffering?
options: It models lament and petition for God’s mercy to restore joy
It denies the possibility of mercy during affliction
It teaches that suffering is always a sign of God’s rejection
It encourages passive acceptance without prayer
questions.correctAnswer: It models lament and petition for God’s mercy to restore joy
questions.explanation: Verses 13-14 show a plea for God to return and satisfy with mercy so that joy may be restored, reflecting biblical patterns of lament and hope.
